identity.name: WATERWAYS LEISURE TOUR L
identity.industry: Consumer Discretionary — Leisure Services / Domestic Cruise Line (India's only scaled home-ported cruise operator)

summary.oneLiner: One of the domestic ocean cruise operators in India (Cordelia Cruises), operating the 'MV Empress' with ~79% value market share in Fiscal 2025.
summary.business: Waterways operates overnight ocean and coastal cruises in India under the Cordelia Cruises brand through a single vessel, the 'MV Empress' (796 cabins, up to ~2,005 guests), sailing domestic destinations (Mumbai, Goa, Kochi, Chennai, Lakshadweep, Visakhapatnam, Puducherry) and international itineraries (Sri Lanka, Maldives, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia). Revenue comes from cabin tickets plus onboard spend (dining, casino, spa, entertainment, MICE/weddings); critical operations (F&B, housekeeping, crewing, entertainment) are outsourced.

endMarkets: Indian leisure/luxury cruise guests and international travellers visiting India|Direct bookings 62.25% (FY26), 62.98% (FY25), 59.96% (FY24) of cabins; balance via travel agents

currentContext.business: Waterways operates overnight ocean and coastal cruises in India under the Cordelia Cruises brand through a single vessel, the 'MV Empress' (796 cabins, up to ~2,005 guests), sailing domestic destinations (Mumbai, Goa, Kochi, Chennai, Lakshadweep, Visakhapatnam, Puducherry) and international itineraries (Sri Lanka, Maldives, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia). Revenue comes from cabin tickets plus onboard spend (dining, casino, spa, entertainment, MICE/weddings); critical operations (F&B, housekeeping, crewing, entertainment) are outsourced.
currentContext.expansion: Waterways intends to expand beyond its single vessel by introducing two additional cruise vessels, 'Norwegian Sky' (capacity up to 2,004 guests) and 'Norwegian Sun' (up to 1,936 guests), and to add new domestic and international itineraries (including Colombo, Sri Lanka and Male, Maldives from Kochi from October 2026), while upgrading dining, cabins and entertainment to meet growing Indian cruise demand supported by the Cruise Bharat Mission.

one-line thesis: A debut earnings call in which demand held up conspicuously well — load factor **105%** (from 99.9%), ticket price +4.3%, guests +~10% — while the entire earnings shortfall came from one line: **fuel**, ~₹14cr of incremental cost after VLSFO spiked from a $580/MT average to $1,228/MT on the West Asia conflict. PAT was ₹22.77cr at ~12% net margin. The real story is capacity: *Cordelia Sky* hands over on 25-Sep-2026 with roughly **double the revenue potential of the Empress** (≈1,000 cabins vs 800, but 269 premium suite/balcony cabins vs 69, nine restaurants vs three), followed by *Cordelia Sun* — turning a single-ship cost structure into a three-ship shared-cost fleet from H2FY27.

|---|---|---|---|

| Finance cost | ~₹4cr | ~doubled YoY | IDFC First Bank loan taken *to establish a credit rating*, fully backed by fixed deposits — economically net-zero-debt |
| Advance bookings (for new ship) | **₹65cr** | — | Management maps this to ~₹110-115cr of revenue on shorter sailings |
> **Adjustments / one-offs:** the margin decline is essentially a single-variable story. CFO: "*the major increase is in the fuel, which is around Rs.14 odd Crores, so if it would have not been there your EBITDA would have gone up by Rs.14 odd Crores.*" The crew-cost increase (~₹2cr, ~16%) is structural, not one-off — it is the first meaningful wage revision for seafarers in ~5 years and reflects international shipping norms. The doubled finance cost is optical: the loan is FD-backed and taken purely to build a rating track record, with prepayment intended once the 1% prepayment cost is worth paying.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Fleet delivery — the hardest dates on the call:** *Cordelia Sky* begins sailing toward India **19-Sep-2026**, **handover 25-Sep-2026**, arrives Mumbai **15-Oct-2026**, **maiden voyage 23-Oct-2026**. *Cordelia Sun* follows (no date given). Management noted a "countdown of 65 days" from the call.
- **Revenue potential of the new ship:** "*the possibility of revenue generating for each ship because of the different cabins and layout is almost 100% increase on potential revenue versus our current vessel.*"
- **Empress like-for-like growth:** ~8-9% currently, "*going forward, it will be 10% to 11% to 12%*" — a double-digit like-for-like guide independent of new capacity.
- **Full-year framing:** "*We expect a year of revenue and earnings growth driven by consumer preference for our cruise brand and expanding our new destinations.*"
- **Fuel recovery:** fuel surcharges are being applied to *new* bookings only (existing bookings are not repriced), so recovery "*will actually show end of Q2, beginning of Q3*"; CEO expects to be "*hopefully eliminating by the end of the year the extra fuel cost*" as VLSFO (now ~$800/MT, down from a $1,228/MT peak) converges toward the forecast price, aided by an efficiency programme that delivered ₹15-16cr of fuel savings last year.
- **Loyalty programme:** "Chairman's Club" rollout **end of Q2 FY27**.
- **Distribution:** new direct-sales centre in **Cochin in September 2026**.
- **Network expansion:** two new islands in **Lakshadweep**; new West Coast ports being tested; **Maldives and Columbus sailings on the East Coast starting October 2026**; **four additional international monsoon sailings from the West Coast from calendar 2027**.
- **Cost structure:** fixed shore-side costs (marketing, management fees) currently absorbed by one ship will be split across two from September and three thereafter, with improved purchasing power — the explicit mechanism for margin expansion.
- **Balance sheet:** intent to prepay the IDFC First Bank loan (carrying it for now because of a 1% prepayment cost and the rating benefit).
order book & pipeline: Not an order-book business; the equivalent is the forward booking curve. **₹65cr of advance bookings already taken for the new ship, which management maps to ₹110-115cr of revenue on shorter sailings.** Booking behaviour: short 2-3 day cruises book 50-60 days out; longer and marquee sailings book far in advance. All "highlight" sailings for *Cordelia Sky* — the maiden voyage, Christmas, New Year, Holi — are **already sold out**, with significant corporate demand. Both new ships have been open for booking since April 2025, well ahead of delivery.
segment / subsidiary detail:
Single operating brand (Cordelia Cruises) under Waterways Leisure Tourism Ltd. Fleet economics dominate the segment discussion:
- **Empress (in service):** ~800 cabins, of which only **69** are suite/balcony (premium); 3 restaurants.
- **Cordelia Sky (Sep-2026):** ~1,000 cabins, of which **~245-269** are suites/balcony; **9 restaurants**; 245 suites. Management is explicit that the revenue uplift comes from **cabin mix, not from pricing** — "*Before we sold 69 rooms every vacation and every cruise for a premium price now we are going to be selling 250 rooms for premium price, on top of it the new ship has 200 rooms more.*"
- **Cordelia Sun:** third vessel, timing not disclosed; completes the three-ship fixed-cost sharing thesis.
Itinerary mix: ~99% of the source-market focus is **visa-free/passport-free** destinations; international sailings target easy-entry destinations for Indians (Sri Lanka, Maldives, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand), including expat-Indian demand.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **International sailings** as the second engine: already tested during this monsoon from the West Coast; four more added from 2027; Maldives and Columbus itineraries on the East Coast from October 2026. Management notes international routes are *cheaper* on port cost than domestic (more sea days between ports, and Indian domestic sailings attract GST on port charges).
- **New Indian ports riding the Cruise Bharat Mission** — Vizag's new cruise terminal, Puducherry, Chennai. Management is deliberately using the weak Q2 season to test these ports at low load factors: "*that is basically an internal investment on building the growth for the next five to six years to come.*"
- **Loyalty and direct distribution** — Chairman's Club from end-Q2, Cochin direct-sales centre in September, multilingual Indian guest engagement — aimed at shifting mix toward direct bookings.
- **Lakshadweep** — two new islands added.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **Structurally advantaged cost base versus global cruise lines operating in India:** management repeatedly framed the business as "*not in the transportation business, we are in the cruising business*," with ~99% of the source market on visa-free/passport-free itineraries — a positioning no international line home-porting in India replicates.
- **Fuel surcharge is a contractual right**, not a negotiation: "*In the airline industry and in the cruise business, we are allowed to take fuel surcharges*" — the cost shock is recoverable on all forward bookings, only the already-sold book is exposed.
- **Demonstrated fuel-efficiency programme** delivering ₹15-16cr of savings in the prior year against forecast price — an operating capability, not a market outcome.
- **First-mover on Indian port infrastructure:** by testing new Cruise Bharat Mission terminals ahead of demand at controlled load factors, the company is establishing itinerary rights and operating knowledge before capacity arrives.
margins & cost dynamics: Fuel is the whole story. VLSFO (a specialised cruise-grade fuel) averaged **$580/MT last year**, peaked at **$1,228/MT** when the West Asia conflict escalated, and sits at **~$800/MT** now. Because fuel is pre-ordered and paid at order price with delivery two to three weeks later, the P&L lags the spot move — management sized the impact as "*65% is secured in the Q3*." Recovery is asymmetric by design: already-sold cruises are not repriced, so surcharges only attach to new bookings, pushing visible recovery to end-Q2/Q3. The second, structural cost line is crew — international-standard seafarer wages rose for the first time in ~5 years, ~₹2cr absolute but ~16% in percentage terms. Food added ~₹1cr. The forward margin lever is not pricing but **operating leverage from fleet scale**: shore-side marketing, management fees and other fixed costs currently carried entirely by one vessel get split across two from September and three thereafter, plus better purchasing power.
capex / expansion (watch slippage): No capex figure was disclosed. The physical expansion programme is expressed entirely in dates: *Cordelia Sky* handover 25-Sep-2026 (currently sailing with guests in Greek/Mediterranean waters), rebranding and India-specific entertainment/guest-offering fit-out immediately after handover, Mumbai arrival 15-Oct-2026, maiden voyage 23-Oct-2026; *Cordelia Sun* thereafter. Shore-side: Cochin sales centre in September; two new Lakshadweep islands; new West Coast ports under test. **Slippage risk is concentrated in the ~3-week window between 25-Sep handover and the 23-Oct maiden voyage**, which has to absorb rebranding, entertainment programme installation and positioning — with marquee sailings already sold.
capital allocation: No dividend/buyback discussion. The only balance-sheet item raised was the **IDFC First Bank loan** — taken deliberately to establish a credit rating because FD-overdraft facilities were not being recognised by rating agencies. It is fully backed by fixed deposits, so the CFO characterises the company as "*technically saying I am zero debt but yes one is standing in the asset side and other standing on the liability side.*" Prepayment is intended, deferred for now against a 1% prepayment cost and the rating benefit. Growth capital is going entirely into fleet and destination expansion.
risks & watch-items:
- **Fuel remains the single dominant swing factor** and is outside management control. The recovery thesis assumes (a) VLSFO keeps converging from $800 toward the forecast price, and (b) surcharges stick on new bookings. Both are hopes with a stated Q3 verification point.
- **Delivery-window compression on Cordelia Sky.** Handover 25-Sep, maiden voyage 23-Oct, with the maiden voyage, Christmas, New Year and Holi sailings already sold. Any slippage in handover, rebranding or fit-out has immediate customer-facing consequences.
- **Q2 is deliberately a weak quarter** — off-season on the West Coast, and management is intentionally running low load factors to test new ports. They frame this as investment and say it will not affect the annual result, but reported Q2 numbers will look poor and should not be read as demand deterioration.
- **First earnings call, thin disclosure.** No revenue figure was stated by management (it had to be inferred), no segmental data, no capex number, no full-year guidance in numbers. The CEO twice declined forward statements ("*Officially, I cannot give you that forward statement*"). Disclosure quality is a genuine watch item for a newly listed company.
- **Crew cost is structurally reset upward** — a 16% increase after five flat years, governed by international shipping regulation rather than local labour markets, and it scales with fleet size.
- **Ramp risk on a much larger vessel.** Sky has ~25% more cabins and ~3.6x the premium cabins; management expects a "three step-up" utilisation path but explicitly would not commit to how long the ramp takes.
- **Concentration:** a single operating vessel today. Until Sky is in service, one ship carries all revenue, all fixed cost and all operational risk.
management quality / tone: Confident, operationally fluent and notably specific on dates — the CEO gave exact handover, arrival and maiden-voyage dates and a fuel price series ($580 average / $1,228 peak / $800 now) rather than deflecting, and explained the mechanics of fuel pre-ordering and surcharge timing in detail unprompted. He also drew a clean line where regulation required it, declining a forward statement on new-ship utilisation ramp. The CFO was similarly direct in decomposing the EBITDA decline into ₹14cr fuel + ₹2cr crew + ₹1cr food, and candid that the IDFC loan exists for rating optics rather than funding need. The weakness is completeness rather than candour: revenue was never stated, no numeric annual guidance was offered, and the "we work on an annual average, do not focus too much on a quarter" framing — reasonable for a seasonal cruise business — will need to be backed by an annual number at some point.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The new-ship revenue uplift is a cabin-mix effect, not a pricing effect.** Same fare categories, same price points — but premium (suite/balcony) inventory goes from 69 to ~250 rooms, plus ~200 additional rooms overall. Modelling the uplift off ticket price rather than mix will materially understate it.
- **A 105% load factor is not an error.** Staterooms carry more than two occupants, so occupancy above 100% is the normal metric for the business — and it rose from 99.9% *during* a fuel-driven price-surcharge period, which is a stronger demand signal than the ~10% guest growth alone conveys.
- **Q2's weakness is manufactured on purpose.** The company is running deliberately low load factors to trial new Cruise Bharat Mission ports (Vizag, Puducherry, Chennai) — treating a soft season as R&D spend for a five-to-six-year destination pipeline rather than chasing quarterly occupancy.
- **International sailings are cheaper to operate than domestic ones**, contrary to intuition: more sea days between ports means fewer port calls per week, and Indian domestic port charges attract GST that international calls do not.
- **The doubled finance cost buys a credit rating, not capital.** The loan is FD-collateralised and economically neutral — a deliberate step to build a rating track record because FD-overdraft facilities were not counted by agencies.

They frame this as investment and say it will not affect the annual result, but reported Q2 numbers will look poor and should not be read as demand deterioration.
- **First earnings call, thin disclosure.** No revenue figure was stated by management (it had to be inferred), no segmental data, no capex number, no full-year guidance in numbers. The CEO twice declined forward statements ("*Officially, I cannot give you that forward statement*"). Disclosure quality is a genuine watch item for a newly listed company.
- **Crew cost is structurally reset upward** — a 16% increase after five flat years, governed by international shipping regulation rather than local labour markets, and it scales with fleet size.
- **Ramp risk on a much larger vessel.** Sky has ~25% more cabins and ~3.6x the premium cabins; management expects a "three step-up" utilisation path but explicitly would not commit to how long the ramp takes.
- **Concentration:** a single operating vessel today. Until Sky is in service, one ship carries all revenue, all fixed cost and all operational risk.
management quality / tone: Confident, operationally fluent and notably specific on dates — the CEO gave exact handover, arrival and maiden-voyage dates and a fuel price series ($580 average / $1,228 peak / $800 now) rather than deflecting, and explained the mechanics of fuel pre-ordering and surcharge timing in detail unprompted. He also drew a clean line where regulation required it, declining a forward statement on new-ship utilisation ramp. The CFO was similarly direct in decomposing the EBITDA decline into ₹14cr fuel + ₹2cr crew + ₹1cr food, and candid that the IDFC loan exists for rating optics rather than funding need. The weakness is completeness rather than candour: revenue was never stated, no numeric annual guidance was offered, and the "we work on an annual average, do not focus too much on a quarter" framing — reasonable for a seasonal cruise business — will need to be backed by an annual number at some point.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The new-ship revenue uplift is a cabin-mix effect, not a pricing effect.** Same fare categories, same price points — but premium (suite/balcony) inventory goes from 69 to ~250 rooms, plus ~200 additional rooms overall. Modelling the uplift off ticket price rather than mix will materially understate it.
- **A 105% load factor is not an error.** Staterooms carry more than two occupants, so occupancy above 100% is the normal metric for the business — and it rose from 99.9% *during* a fuel-driven price-surcharge period, which is a stronger demand signal than the ~10% guest growth alone conveys.

- **International sailings are cheaper to operate than domestic ones**, contrary to intuition: more sea days between ports means fewer port calls per week, and Indian domestic port charges attract GST that international calls do not.
- **The doubled finance cost buys a credit rating, not capital.** The loan is FD-collateralised and economically neutral — a deliberate step to build a rating track record because FD-overdraft facilities were not counted by agencies.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: One of the domestic ocean cruise operators in India (Cordelia Cruises), operating the 'MV Empress' with ~79% value market share in Fiscal 2025.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Waterways operates overnight ocean and coastal cruises in India under the Cordelia Cruises brand through a single vessel, the 'MV Empress' (796 cabins, up to ~2,005 guests), sailing domestic destinations (Mumbai, Goa, Kochi, Chennai, Lakshadweep, Visakhapatnam, Puducherry) and international itineraries (Sri Lanka, Maldives, Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia). Revenue comes from cabin tickets plus onboard spend (dining, casino, spa, entertainment, MICE/weddings); critical operations (F&B, housekeeping, crewing, entertainment) are outsourced.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)
group_structure.body:
- Bay Cruise Investment Inc. (BCII) — Wholly-owned subsidiary (100% from Feb 28, 2025): Owns the vessel MV Empress; acquired via investment agreement dated Feb 17, 2025
- Baycruise Shipping and Leasing (IFSC) Private Limited — Step-down subsidiary (IFSC leasing entity): Recipient of IPO-funded deposit/advance lease rental and monthly lease payments (Rs 4,800.10 million)
- Global Shipping and Leisure Limited — Corporate Promoter (Mauritius)

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body:
Single operating brand (Cordelia Cruises) under Waterways Leisure Tourism Ltd. Fleet economics dominate the segment discussion:
- **Empress (in service):** ~800 cabins, of which only **69** are suite/balcony (premium); 3 restaurants.
- **Cordelia Sky (Sep-2026):** ~1,000 cabins, of which **~245-269** are suites/balcony; **9 restaurants**; 245 suites. Management is explicit that the revenue uplift comes from **cabin mix, not from pricing** — "*Before we sold 69 rooms every vacation and every cruise for a premium price now we are going to be selling 250 rooms for premium price, on top of it the new ship has 200 rooms more.*"
- **Cordelia Sun:** third vessel, timing not disclosed; completes the three-ship fixed-cost sharing thesis.
Itinerary mix: ~99% of the source-market focus is **visa-free/passport-free** destinations; international sailings target easy-entry destinations for Indians (Sri Lanka, Maldives, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand), including expat-Indian demand.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Cruise cabins:** 1 Chairman's suite (Rs 151,111/night), 5 suites, 63 mini suites, 416 ocean-view staterooms, 311 interior staterooms (from Rs 34,164/night), Total 796 cabins on MV Empress
- **Onboard & ancillary:** Dining (pan-Asian, international, Indian, Jain), Casino, spa & salon, theatre, gaming arcade, fitness, rock-climbing, pools, MICE events and weddings

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Indian leisure/luxury cruise guests and international travellers visiting India
- Direct bookings 62.25% (FY26), 62.98% (FY25), 59.96% (FY24) of cabins; balance via travel agents

cost_leadership.title: Supply chain integration (RHP report)
cost_leadership.body: Asset structure: vessel MV Empress owned via wholly-owned subsidiary Bay Cruise Investment Inc.; two new vessels (Norwegian Sky, Norwegian Sun) chartered from step-down subsidiary Baycruise Shipping and Leasing (IFSC) Private Limited under Time Charter Agreements. Critical cruise operations (food & beverage, housekeeping, crewing, entertainment) are outsourced to third parties to enable scalability and manage seasonal demand. Key third-party service providers named: SA Cruise Services Limited, Apollo Export Warehouse LLC (with Indian arm Asturias Ship Chandlers Private Limited), Campbell Cruise & Yacht Management Limited and Wizcraft Entertainment Agency Private Limited. Direct bookings supported by a 148-person call-centre team.

order_book.title: Order book & pipeline
order_book.body: Not an order-book business; the equivalent is the forward booking curve. **₹65cr of advance bookings already taken for the new ship, which management maps to ₹110-115cr of revenue on shorter sailings.** Booking behaviour: short 2-3 day cruises book 50-60 days out; longer and marquee sailings book far in advance. All "highlight" sailings for *Cordelia Sky* — the maiden voyage, Christmas, New Year, Holi — are **already sold out**, with significant corporate demand. Both new ships have been open for booking since April 2025, well ahead of delivery.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
- **Fleet delivery — the hardest dates on the call:** *Cordelia Sky* begins sailing toward India **19-Sep-2026**, **handover 25-Sep-2026**, arrives Mumbai **15-Oct-2026**, **maiden voyage 23-Oct-2026**. *Cordelia Sun* follows (no date given). Management noted a "countdown of 65 days" from the call.
- **Revenue potential of the new ship:** "*the possibility of revenue generating for each ship because of the different cabins and layout is almost 100% increase on potential revenue versus our current vessel.*"
- **Empress like-for-like growth:** ~8-9% currently, "*going forward, it will be 10% to 11% to 12%*" — a double-digit like-for-like guide independent of new capacity.
- **Full-year framing:** "*We expect a year of revenue and earnings growth driven by consumer preference for our cruise brand and expanding our new destinations.*"
- **Fuel recovery:** fuel surcharges are being applied to *new* bookings only (existing bookings are not repriced), so recovery "*will actually show end of Q2, beginning of Q3*"; CEO expects to be "*hopefully eliminating by the end of the year the extra fuel cost*" as VLSFO (now ~$800/MT, down from a $1,228/MT peak) converges toward the forecast price, aided by an efficiency programme that delivered ₹15-16cr of fuel savings last year.
- **Loyalty programme:** "Chairman's Club" rollout **end of Q2 FY27**.
- **Distribution:** new direct-sales centre in **Cochin in September 2026**.
- **Network expansion:** two new islands in **Lakshadweep**; new West Coast ports being tested; **Maldives and Columbus sailings on the East Coast starting October 2026**; **four additional international monsoon sailings from the West Coast from calendar 2027**.
- **Cost structure:** fixed shore-side costs (marketing, management fees) currently absorbed by one ship will be split across two from September and three thereafter, with improved purchasing power — the explicit mechanism for margin expansion.
- **Balance sheet:** intent to prepay the IDFC First Bank loan (carrying it for now because of a 1% prepayment cost and the rating benefit).

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **International sailings** as the second engine: already tested during this monsoon from the West Coast; four more added from 2027; Maldives and Columbus itineraries on the East Coast from October 2026. Management notes international routes are *cheaper* on port cost than domestic (more sea days between ports, and Indian domestic sailings attract GST on port charges).
- **New Indian ports riding the Cruise Bharat Mission** — Vizag's new cruise terminal, Puducherry, Chennai. Management is deliberately using the weak Q2 season to test these ports at low load factors: "*that is basically an internal investment on building the growth for the next five to six years to come.*"
- **Loyalty and direct distribution** — Chairman's Club from end-Q2, Cochin direct-sales centre in September, multilingual Indian guest engagement — aimed at shifting mix toward direct bookings.
- **Lakshadweep** — two new islands added.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Ability to introduce new cruise vessels to meet growing demand (currently single-vessel operations)
- Passenger load factor / occupancy (91.63% FY25, 84.99% FY26) and average ticket price / revenue per passenger
- Fuel cost per passenger cruise day (Rs 1,480.33 FY26)
- Direct-booking mix reducing agent commissions
- Cruise industry cyclicality (India market declined ~12% in FY26 due to macro/fuel/geopolitical headwinds)

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body: Fuel is the whole story. VLSFO (a specialised cruise-grade fuel) averaged **$580/MT last year**, peaked at **$1,228/MT** when the West Asia conflict escalated, and sits at **~$800/MT** now. Because fuel is pre-ordered and paid at order price with delivery two to three weeks later, the P&L lags the spot move — management sized the impact as "*65% is secured in the Q3*." Recovery is asymmetric by design: already-sold cruises are not repriced, so surcharges only attach to new bookings, pushing visible recovery to end-Q2/Q3. The second, structural cost line is crew — international-standard seafarer wages rose for the first time in ~5 years, ~₹2cr absolute but ~16% in percentage terms. Food added ~₹1cr. The forward margin lever is not pricing but **operating leverage from fleet scale**: shore-side marketing, management fees and other fixed costs currently carried entirely by one vessel get split across two from September and three thereafter, plus better purchasing power.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: No dividend/buyback discussion. The only balance-sheet item raised was the **IDFC First Bank loan** — taken deliberately to establish a credit rating because FD-overdraft facilities were not being recognised by rating agencies. It is fully backed by fixed deposits, so the CFO characterises the company as "*technically saying I am zero debt but yes one is standing in the asset side and other standing on the liability side.*" Prepayment is intended, deferred for now against a 1% prepayment cost and the rating benefit. Growth capital is going entirely into fleet and destination expansion.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Waterways intends to expand beyond its single vessel by introducing two additional cruise vessels, 'Norwegian Sky' (capacity up to 2,004 guests) and 'Norwegian Sun' (up to 1,936 guests), and to add new domestic and international itineraries (including Colombo, Sri Lanka and Male, Maldives from Kochi from October 2026), while upgrading dining, cabins and entertainment to meet growing Indian cruise demand supported by the Cruise Bharat Mission.

The weakness is completeness rather than candour: revenue was never stated, no numeric annual guidance was offered, and the "we work on an annual average, do not focus too much on a quarter" framing — reasonable for a seasonal cruise business — will need to be backed by an annual number at some point.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Pioneer / leading domestic ocean cruise operator in India with ~79% value market share in FY25 (CRISIL)
- Single premium vessel MV Empress with 796 cabins and diverse onboard amenities; 730,819 guests carried since launch
- High direct-booking mix (~62% of cabins) reducing agent commissions and improving margins; 148-strong call-centre team
- Experienced cruise-industry management (Chairman/CEO Jurgen Bailom, founding member of the Indian Cruise Lines Association)
- Industry tailwinds: Cruise Bharat Mission targeting doubling of cruise passenger traffic by 2029; very low India cruise penetration (0.01% vs 5.7% North America)

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Fuel remains the single dominant swing factor** and is outside management control. The recovery thesis assumes (a) VLSFO keeps converging from $800 toward the forecast price, and (b) surcharges stick on new bookings. Both are hopes with a stated Q3 verification point.
- **Delivery-window compression on Cordelia Sky.** Handover 25-Sep, maiden voyage 23-Oct, with the maiden voyage, Christmas, New Year and Holi sailings already sold. Any slippage in handover, rebranding or fit-out has immediate customer-facing consequences.

commitments.title: Promises (RHP)
commitments.body:
- **Introduce two new cruise vessels, 'Norwegian Sky' and 'Norwegian Sun'**
- **Introduce new itineraries to Colombo (Sri Lanka) and Male (Maldives) from Kochi**
- **Deploy IPO proceeds toward deposit/advance lease rental and monthly lease payments to step-down subsidiary Baycruise IFSC**

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Introduce two new cruise vessels, 'Norwegian Sky' (up to 2,004 guests) and 'Norwegian Sun' (up to 1,936 guests), to expand fleet capacity

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Corporate status] The issuer is Waterways Leisure Tourism Limited, "formerly known as Waterways Leisure Tourism Private Limited" (CIN U63030MH2020PLC440323), registered in Mumbai, listed with BSE scrip code 544802 and NSE symbol CORDELIA.
- [Reporting basis] All figures are "derived from the Company's internal Operating Profit Analysis and its restated statutory financial statements", presented in INR Millions, with prior-period figures "regrouped and/or reclassified wherever considered necessary".
- [Revenue definition] Gross Ticket Revenue of Rs 2,082.6 million is stated as "incl. of GST" (up 10% vs. Q1 FY26), and is defined separately from Net Revenue, which is "Gross Ticket revenue excluding GST" - the two must not be read as the same figure.
- [Standalone vs consolidated] The headline quarter-at-a-glance metrics are marked "* Consolidated Financial Results", while the financial summary presents standalone and consolidated side by side with materially different finance cost, depreciation, EBITDA and PAT, so the two bases must be kept apart.
- [Internal inconsistency] The consolidated Q1 FY27 EBITDA margin is shown as "24.5% EBITDA margin" on the quarter-at-a-glance slide and as "465.31 - 24%" in the financial summary table; both readings are as printed.
